item.title: Int'l expeditions in China unlock secrets of Asia's longest cave
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
GUIYANG, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- For French caver Jean Bottazzi, caves never disappoint. In the vast underground maze of Shuanghe Cave in southwest China's Guizhou Province, even an unfinished mission can lead to an unexpected discovery, opening up whole new horizons. Bottazzi has spent more than two decades exploring Shuanghe, witnessing its 25-year journey of international exploration. Situated in Suiyang County, it is the world's third-longest cave system and Asia's longest. Since the first China-France joint exploration in 2001, the mapped cave system has expanded from several dozen kilometers of known passages to more than 480 kilometers. The latest findings from the 25th international cave scientific expedition were announced last month in Suiyang. Another 41.8 kilometers were added to the mapped passages. With the newly added length, the cave system now stretches 481.5 kilometers and reaches a vertical depth of 912 meters. It has 124 interconnected entrances. For Bottazzi, as well as the scientists and explorers who have worked alongside him, the significance of Shuanghe Cave cannot be measured by its length alone. It is also a vast natural archive that preserves clues to the evolution of species, the changing climate and the geological history of southwest China. Researchers found nine additional individual giant panda fossils, mostly in newly explored passages, during the 25th international expedition this year, bringing the total number of individual giant panda fossils discovered in Shuanghe Cave to 61. They also found two sites bearing clear giant panda claw marks. Wang Deyuan, an associate research fellow at the Guizhou Academy of Sciences' Institute of Mountain Resources, said the marks and the structure of the cave passages offer clues to how some of the animals may have died. The pandas apparently entered the cave and moved more than 10 meters inward before falling into a vertical shaft. They survived the initial fall and left claw marks as they tried to move on, but eventually fell into a deeper shaft and became trapped, Wang said. The latest expedition also uncovered fossils of ancient animals. Among them, fossils of a giant tapir and a clouded leopard were found in Shuanghe Cave for the first time. For Bottazzi, however, the fascination of cave exploration lies not only in what researchers find, but also in what they do not expect to find. A recent expedition experience reminded Bottazzi once again why he fell in love with caves in the first place. The team had set out to connect several caves at the northern end of the Shuanghe Cave system, but the goal remained elusive. However, the story didn't end there. As they groped their way forward, something entirely unexpected appeared before them -- an entire magnificent wall of gypsum crystals. "Curiosity instantly rekindled a new thrill of exploration and unexpectedly opened up a new direction," Bottazzi recalled. "If we had focused only on our planned goal, we would never have met this surprise. Half disappointment, half satisfaction -- that is the true charm of cave exploration," he said. The Shuanghe Cave also serves as an archive with hidden clues to ancient climate. Researchers have been conducting uranium-series dating of calcite deposits inside the cave, according to Bottazzi. "As long as we can find calcite samples of different ages and combine them with isotope analysis, we can obtain a record of climate evolution from the present day all the way back a million years," Bottazzi said. "It is an extremely precious archive of paleoclimate." The line of research made a breakthrough this year. Using the new uranium-lead isotope dating technique, the research team determined that some secondary carbonate deposits inside the cave are more than five million years old. The finding significantly extends the chronological framework for the development of Shuanghe Cave and other large caves in the karst regions of southwest China. The vast underground maze of Shuanghe Cave has not only yielded a string of discoveries that have captivated the scientific world, but also become a vivid example of international cooperation in cave research. Asked how Chinese and foreign researchers share exploration data and cave maps, Bottazzi was unequivocal: "We work for science. All the data and cave maps are shared." For Bottazzi, the cave has continued to captivate him so deeply that in recent years he settled in Shuanghe Village in Wenquan Township, Suiyang. Over the years, he has become such a familiar face in the village that locals affectionately call him "Lao Rang," or "Old Jean." To Bottazzi, there are few better places than Shuanghe to explore the Earth's hidden treasures. The cave is a world of diverse landscapes, from underground rivers and vast chambers draped with waterfalls to completely dry fossil galleries. "We are exploring as if inside a maze; you can never guess where the passage leads, and you have to keep thinking. For cave exploration, this is a wonderfully fascinating place," Bottazzi said. ■

item.title: China's cat parks seek lasting, sustainable homes for strays
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
Cats are seen at Chongqing Firefly Bay Cat Harbor Park in Chongqing, southwest China, Oct. 4, 2026. (Xinhua/Wu Yanxia) CHONGQING/HARBIN, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- When Chongqing Firefly Bay Cat Harbor Park opened on New Year's Day in southwest China, it had just over 600 cats. More than eight months later, the number has passed 1,000. By September, the 30,000-square-meter riverside park had rescued or taken in more than 1,300 cats, while over 240 had been adopted. As the number of cats grows, so do the demands on the park -- from veterinary care and staffing to finding enough space for new arrivals. "The first thing is to keep the daily operation running," said Jian Ning, who oversees offline operations at the park. "We have to survive first before talking about anything else." The park sits on what was a long-idle site near Nanbin Road in Chongqing Municipality. The local government provides the land rent-free, while the operator earns revenue from admission fees, spending inside the park and rent paid by businesses on the site. A ticket costs 19.9 yuan (about 3 U.S. dollars). During the city's hot summer, when fewer people visit the outdoor park, daily attendance averages just over 300. On its busiest day, however, the park received 8,000 visitors. Veterinary care accounts for roughly one-third of operating costs, Jian said. Current revenue is enough to keep the park running day to day, but making a profit remains difficult. "If we had to pay normal rent, the operating pressure would be much greater," Jian said. The park now employs 51 people, including animal-care staff, security guards and cleaners. Most employees who work directly with the cats are in their 20s. All are paid, full-time staff. "We don't expect people to work simply for love," Jian said. Most members of the park's core team are from stray-cat rescue groups. They had seen rescue efforts struggle with a basic problem: expenses kept mounting, while funding often depended on donations, subsidies or rescuers paying out of their own pockets. The team therefore decided to open the site to visitors, hoping revenue from ticket sales and other businesses could help cover the cost of long-term care for rescued cats. The park sums up the idea in a lighthearted slogan: "Cats work to support themselves." The experiment is unfolding alongside a sizable pet economy. China had 126 million pet dogs and cats in urban areas in 2025, including 72.89 million cats, while the urban dog-and-cat consumer market reached 312.6 billion yuan, according to the 2026 China Pet Industry White Paper (Consumption Report). Yet space has a limit. Jian estimated that the park could accommodate 2,000 to 3,000 cats. If the population approaches that level, she said, new admissions will have to be reduced. The park does not encourage people to relocate stray cats that are regularly fed in residential communities, as they have already grown accustomed to those surroundings, Jian said. Scientific research also suggests that managing free-roaming cat populations requires more than one-off interventions. A 12-year controlled study published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found that sustained, high-intensity neutering across contiguous areas could reduce cat numbers, while immigration and other compensatory effects could weaken the impact. The researchers recommended combining the trap-neuter-return method with complementary measures such as adoption and resource management. Adoption certainly provides another outlet. Applicants face strict requirements, however, and the park conducts follow-up checks. None of the more than 240 adopted cats have so far been returned. Visitors, meanwhile, must adapt to rules designed around the animals. Children under six are not admitted, and staff ask visitors not to chase cats or pick them up against their will. Jian said disputes over scratches and bites have become less common as visitor guidance has improved. The park may stop admitting visitors once more than 3,000 people are inside. So far, the flow of people in and out has made that unnecessary. Some 3,000 kilometers away in northeast China, another cat park is testing a similar combination of animal rescue and tourism on a smaller scale. Scarlett's Friends, Heilongjiang Province's first cat-themed park, opened on Aug. 28 at the Yabuli Ski Resort in Harbin and is now home to 150 rescued stray cats. The cat park occupies a site that had stood idle for years and gives Yabuli, long known for winter skiing, another attraction for the warmer months. Before entering areas open to visitors, the cats must be neutered, vaccinated, treated for parasites, and assessed to determine whether they can adapt to interaction with people. Sick cats are moved to an isolation area, while a partner veterinary hospital provides regular health support. Winter in Yabuli brings temperatures far below freezing. Indoor activity areas and cat houses have been equipped with air-source heating systems, and the cats will spend most of the winter indoors, said Liu Guangpeng, deputy general manager of Harbin Yabuli Tourism Investment Group Co., Ltd. Ning Xiaofeng, general manager of the group, said stray-cat rescue that relies solely on continued spending is difficult to sustain. By linking the park with tourism, the operator aims to use tourism revenue to help cover the cost of caring for the cats while providing them with a stable home. Liu said the park would limit visitor numbers rather than compromise the cats' welfare. "Even if there were no visitors, we would still make sure the cats were properly cared for," he said. If crowds exceeded the park's capacity, it would introduce reservations and limit entry. Similar ideas have begun to appear in local policies. In February, the eastern Chinese city of Nanjing in Jiangsu Province issued guidelines encouraging pet-related tourism while calling for stray animals to be managed via capture, neutering, return or adoption. The document also said eligible animal-protection groups could receive support through government service purchases and public-interest programs. Back in Chongqing, Jian explained that relying entirely on subsidies, donations or unpaid work would not be sustainable. "Only by using commercial operations to support rescue can we keep this going in the long run," she said. During Chongqing's hot summer, the park stays open until midnight. As temperatures fall in the evening, visitors arrive to see the cats and enjoy the riverside night view. Many simply sit and wait. "Here, you don't have to talk or please anyone," Jian said. "You can just sit on the steps, and maybe a cat will come over, rub against you or fall asleep in your lap." ■ Tourists interact with cats at Chongqing Firefly Bay Cat Harbor Park in Chongqing, southwest China, Oct. 4, 2026. (Xinhua/Wu Yanxia) Tourists visit Chongqing Firefly Bay Cat Harbor Park in Chongqing, southwest China, Oct. 4, 2026. (Xinhua/Wu Yanxia)

item.title: From import replacement to global exporter, Chinese harvester maker sweetens sugarcane business
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
by Xinhua writer Zhang Yunlong ZHENGZHOU, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- "People say a woman fears marrying the wrong man, while a man fears choosing the wrong trade. I definitely chose the wrong trade," Zhang Changxian, 59, said with a laugh. When Zhang began developing a sugarcane harvester in 2008, he expected challenges. He did not expect it would take eight years to bring the machine to market. For years, the engineer-turned-entrepreneur and his team spent harvest seasons testing and redesigning prototypes in cane fields in Chongzuo, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. The city is about 1,600 km from his factory in Luoyang, central China's Henan Province. During one field test, a steering linkage snapped in a muddy patch. In many others, the machine struggled with cane flattened by typhoons. Today, machines made by his company, Luoyang Chenhan Agricultural Equipment Technology, account for about half of China's sugarcane harvester market by volume, the company says. They are also drawing buyers overseas, from Southeast Asia to Latin America. The company's rise comes as China's sugar industry seeks to cut costs and improve competitiveness through mechanization. China has long relied on imports to bridge a wide gap between domestic sugar output and demand. In the 2024/25 marketing year, the country produced about 11.2 million tonnes of sugar and consumed about 15.7 million tonnes, according to the Chinese Agriculture Outlook Committee under the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs. Imports totaled about 4.6 million tonnes. According to Zhang, major sugar-exporting countries such as Brazil generally enjoy lower production costs, with large-scale mechanized farming being one of the key factors. Rising labor costs have added to the pressure on China's sugar industry. When Zhang entered the industry in 2008, a worker could harvest about one tonne of cane a day for 25 to 30 yuan (3.7 to 4.5 U.S. dollars). Today, the same work can cost 180 to 250 yuan, he said, while harvested cane sells for around 500 yuan a tonne. As labor costs climb, demand for mechanized harvesting has grown. One Chenhan harvester, Zhang said, can now cut more than 100 tonnes of cane a day, roughly the work of 100 laborers. When Zhang started, nearly all harvesters in China were imported. His team decided to develop equipment tailored to local conditions. But building a domestic harvester proved far harder than many had expected. Unlike in Brazil and Australia, where cane is often grown on large plantations, China's major sugarcane regions typically have sloping terrain, with smaller and more fragmented fields. Many major agricultural machinery makers focused on larger markets for wheat, corn and rice equipment, while sugarcane harvesting was a niche segment with significant technical challenges. With no established supply chains or mature domestic components for sugarcane harvesters at the time, Zhang's team had to design and test many critical systems themselves. Each year offered only a narrow testing window because cane is harvested in a specific season, so a design flaw found in the field often meant waiting another year for large-scale trials. After nearly three years without a breakthrough, Zhang put the project on hold for a while. Experts, including his former mentor, advised him to give up, he recalled. A turning point came in 2011 when the team resumed work and shifted from an earlier whole-stalk harvesting approach to a chopped-cane system better suited to Chinese field conditions. "At times we nearly ran out of money," Zhang said. To keep going, he used money set aside for his daughter's education and later mortgaged property to fund development. Chenhan completed its first harvester in 2015. The machine entered the market a year later and sold more than 30 units in 2016, rising to more than 150 the following year. Overseas expansion began in 2019. The company has since exported machines to countries including Vietnam, Thailand, Indonesia, Costa Rica and Venezuela. Exports account for about one-fifth of revenue and are growing steadily, Zhang said. Many foreign buyers are drawn by lower prices and the company's willingness to customize equipment. Customers in the French overseas department of Reunion, for example, requested tracked harvesters able to work on volcanic soil. The company developed a specialized tracked machine to reduce ground pressure and optimized its cooling systems for the island's tropical climate. Looking ahead, Zhang said the company is exploring smarter controls, hybrid power systems and lower fuel consumption. "Many people told us Chinese companies couldn't make a sugarcane harvester," Zhang said, recalling the early doubts. "We made it, and now we're exporting it." ■

item.title: Why G7 agrees to release fuel reserves, how helpful will it be?
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
BRUSSELS, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Group of Seven (G7) leaders agreed Friday to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves in an action coordinated through the International Energy Agency (IEA), as surging fuel prices, disrupted refined-product supplies and threatened U.S. export restrictions added pressure on global energy markets. Under the agreement, the 100 million barrels will be released over four months, starting immediately, with a substantial amount of diesel to be frontloaded within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners. The G7 did not specify how much of the total would be diesel or crude oil, or how many individual countries would contribute. It said further diesel releases could be considered if necessary. IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said Friday that around 325 million barrels have so far been released under the collective action announced in March, representing more than 80 percent of the 400 million barrels originally pledged, the largest move of its kind in the agency's history. The group also agreed to coordinate refinery maintenance to avoid simultaneous shutdowns, temporarily raise refinery utilization where possible and encourage countries with significant refining capacity to increase production, particularly of diesel. Pressure has been acute in global fuel markets, particularly diesel, as two major sources of diesel and gasoil supply have been hit at the same time. Net diesel and gasoil exports from Gulf countries averaged just slightly more than a quarter of pre-U.S.-Iran war levels, as flows through the Strait of Hormuz remained severely constrained, according to the IEA. Birol also said that Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have added to the pressure on diesel supplies, pushing up prices. Europe has felt the strain acutely. The European Commission said Friday that diesel prices had doubled since the end of February when the U.S.-Iran war started, contributing to what it described as an "affordability crisis." EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen said Tuesday that the bloc had paid more than 100 billion euros (about 113.3 billion U.S. dollars) extra for fossil fuel imports since the start of the U.S.-Iran conflict, without receiving additional energy. The decision also followed mounting transatlantic friction over how to respond. The Trump administration had pressed European governments to draw down more emergency diesel stocks and warned that restrictions on U.S. diesel exports could follow if Europe did not act. The threat carried weight for Europe. The European Commission said last week that the United States accounted for around half of EU diesel imports in August, making the bloc highly exposed to any disruption in U.S. supplies. Hours before the G7 agreement, the Commission publicly rejected the prospect of a U.S. diesel export ban, saying such a move would benefit neither side and undermine trust in the United States as a reliable partner. The eventual G7 agreement combined coordinated reserve releases with a commitment to refrain from restricting energy exports among members, a move later welcomed by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Analysts say the release could provide meaningful short-term relief, particularly if large diesel volumes reach the market quickly. Alan Gelder, senior vice president for refining, chemicals and oil markets at Wood Mackenzie, estimated that a major diesel stock release could lower wholesale prices by 20 to 30 U.S. dollars per barrel. But the effect may prove temporary. Gelder said further stock releases essentially buy time while global diesel supply remains below demand and inventories continue to be drawn down, adding that the EU continues to be vulnerable to the export policies of others such as the United States. Ultimately, the longer-term stability of prices will depend on the restoration of refined-product flows from the Middle East. But with the U.S.-Iran conflict proving difficult to resolve, a swift return to more stable flows may remain out of reach. ■

item.title: China sets sight on LA after record 169 golds at Asian Games: delegation official
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- China delivered an outstanding performance at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games and accomplished its mission of preparing for the Los Angeles Olympics, Zhang Xin, secretary-general of the Chinese delegation, said in a statement on Sunday. China topped both the gold and the overall medal table for the 12th consecutive Asian Games, winning 169 golds, 89 silvers and 83 bronzes for a total of 341 medals, a record gold-medal haul for China at an Asian Games held outside China. Zhang noted the delegation's performance in Nagoya showed four main characteristics. Zhang said China's leading position in Asian sport was further consolidated. The delegation competed in 369 of the Games' events across 38 sports and 59 disciplines, winning gold in 38 of those disciplines and medals in 47, despite fielding fewer athletes and entries than at the previous Games in Hangzhou and facing a reduced number of medal events to contest. The quality of China's results was also notable, Zhang said, with Chinese athletes breaking five world records, 11 Asian records and 22 Games records in sports with recognized records, including shooting, archery, athletics, swimming, weightlifting and track cycling. "Winning performances in the women's javelin and hammer throw matched the gold-medal standards set at the Paris Olympics, while China's men's 200m freestyle, men's 4x100m medley relay and women's 200m individual medley all produced the world's best times so far this year," it read. China also made gains in sports where it has traditionally lagged, according to Zhang. Triathlon delivered the country's best-ever Asian Games results across all three events, breaking Japan's long-standing dominance of the sport in Asia. The equestrian team won its first-ever Asian Games gold in team dressage, while China reclaimed the road cycling title after a 20-year gap and the men's individual modern pentathlon gold after 12 years. Zhang stated that a new generation of Chinese athletes also emerged at the Games. Of the delegation's 815 athletes, 548, or around two-thirds, were competing at their first Asian Games. "17-year-old Chen Yujie became Asia's youngest women's 100m champion, while 18-year-old Yan Ziyi won javelin gold with a single throw. 14-year-old Yu Zidi claimed three swimming golds, each breaking an Asian or Games record, and 19-year-old Zhang Zhanshuo equaled the Games record for individual gold medals at a single edition with seven swimming titles," he said. Looking ahead to the Los Angeles Olympics, Zhang said the Nagoya Games had served its purpose. "At this Asian Games, we have achieved our goals of testing our team, discovering new talent, identifying problems and conducting comprehensive training, further strengthening our confidence in achieving outstanding results at the Los Angeles Olympics," he said. "After the Nagoya Asian Games, we will immediately shift to preparations for the Los Angeles Olympics, accelerate efforts to address our weaknesses, comprehensively improve our competitive level, and go all out to meet the challenge of the Los Angeles Olympics," Zhang added. ■

item.title: China trade ties carry significant weight for U.S. West Coast ports
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
by Julia Pierrepont III, Gao Shan LOS ANGELES, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- With China accounting for about 55 percent of trade at the Port of Long Beach and roughly 40 percent of business at the neighboring Port of Los Angeles, stable relations between Washington and Beijing are not an abstract diplomatic concern for the two busiest container ports in the United States. That deep trade linkage means shifts in U.S.-China ties can quickly ripple through cargo flows, jobs, consumer supply chains and investment across Southern California, according to the heads of the two ports. "Stable and constructive relations between the United States and China are important to the global economy, to American consumers and businesses, and to the reliability of international supply chains," Noel Hacegaba, CEO of the Port of Long Beach, told Xinhua. The two ports, located side by side in San Pedro Bay, form the largest container gateway in the United States and anchor a vast logistics network of dockworkers, truckers, warehouses, railroads, retailers and exporters. China has been Long Beach's largest trading partner by cargo volume for decades and now accounts for about 55 percent of the port's imports and exports, Hacegaba said. He described Long Beach as "a vital link in the Pacific trade corridor," connecting Chinese manufacturers and exporters with U.S. consumers, businesses and distribution networks, while also serving as a gateway for California goods headed to China. At the Port of Los Angeles, ties with China are similarly deep. Gene Seroka, the port's executive director, said China accounts for approximately 40 percent of its business, more than two and a half times that of its next-largest trading partner. "China remains a critically important trading partner for the Port of Los Angeles, and our longstanding relationships with Chinese ports have opened the door to cooperation that goes well beyond moving cargo," Seroka said. Trade with China remains central to both ports. A more stable bilateral relationship would help protect cargo flows, jobs and consumer supply chains. China is also one of the leading export markets for California goods, Hacegaba said. Beyond cargo volumes, the ports are expanding cooperation with Chinese counterparts in areas including cleaner shipping, digitalization and supply-chain resilience. Seroka cited work with the ports of Shanghai, Guangzhou and, more recently, Shenzhen on green shipping corridors and other initiatives aimed at cutting emissions and making global trade more efficient and resilient. "These port-to-port partnerships are a good example of how practical cooperation can deliver meaningful benefits on both sides of the Pacific," he said. As the Port of Los Angeles handles more than 10 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) annually, while the Port of Long Beach processed a record 9.9 million TEUs in 2025, the scale of the two ports underscores the wider economic stakes. Together, they handled about 31 percent of U.S. containerized international waterborne trade in 2025 and support 2.4 million jobs nationwide. ■

item.title: Over 300 artifacts, documents debut in Beijing as China marks 90th anniversary of Long March victory
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
BEIJING, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- More than 300 artifacts and historical documents related to the Long March are being exhibited for the first time at a military museum in Beijing, offering new details about an event that helped shape the history of the 20th century. The exhibition comes as China marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, which concluded in October 1936 when the main forces of the Red Army broke through the siege of the Kuomintang forces and reunited in northwest China. The military odyssey of roughly 12,500 kilometers, which started in 1934, not only preserved the revolutionary forces, but also gave the Communist Party of China (CPC) a new foothold from which to grow the strength of the revolution, and a new starting point from which to carry the revolution forward to victory. One highlight of the exhibition is a collection of manuscripts recounting battles, radio communications, daily experiences and other aspects of the journey. Some were written by the individuals themselves, while most were compiled from their oral accounts. These manuscripts offer valuable firsthand records, while also displaying literary merit, said a guide at the Military Museum of the Chinese People's Revolution, which is hosting the themed exhibition. Among them is a manuscript by a division commander, recounting how his unit tried to hold back enemy forces at the Xiangjiang River in late 1934. Historical records show that the Central Red Army emerged from the campaign with just over 30,000 troops, down from more than 86,000 at the start of the Long March. An exhibition curator at the museum said that the newly displayed materials, along with the personal belongings of those who died in battle, help broaden knowledge of what happened in key battles during the Long March. They also provide valuable source material for research into military history. Over the past nine decades, the Long March has drawn journalists, writers and scholars from around the world to retrace its route and explore its history as a way to understand the CPC and China today. More than a strategic military maneuver, it is widely regarded as a saga of ideals, devotion, willpower and bravery. Another group of newly displayed artifacts offers a glimpse into how Red Army soldiers pushed the limits of human endurance in some of the most unforgiving terrain along the route. They include a blue, single-layer coat and a simple knitted blanket used by soldiers to keep warm while crossing snow-covered mountains, as well as everyday items such as a fire-starting tool and a first-aid pouch. According to information presented at the exhibition, the main forces of the Red Army climbed more than 20 snow-covered mountains rising above 4,000 meters during the Long March. Thin air, deep ravines and rapidly changing weather made the journey a constant test of endurance. Some soldiers collapsed from exhaustion, while others froze to death. Hundreds of kilometers of marshland posed another formidable challenge for the Red Army. The terrain was so treacherous that it was described as a "death trap," with hidden marshes that could swallow people and animals without warning. Many soldiers lost their lives there. Some died of illness or starvation, while others were poisoned by wild plants they ate in a desperate bid to survive. Others simply disappeared in the marshes. The exhibition in Beijing features newly displayed artifacts from this ordeal, including half of a belt, with the other half having been eaten by a soldier, a fishing line used by a senior officer to catch fish for food, and straw sandals reinforced with cloth that soldiers wore while crossing the marshlands. Keith Bennett, international relations consultant and vice president of the London-based 48 Group, pointed to conviction, discipline and perseverance as enduring values of the Long March, saying they continue to inspire China's modernization and its vision of multipolarity, global cooperation and shared progress. The spirit of the Long March, he said, remains a living force in contemporary China, guiding endeavors like poverty alleviation, rural revitalization, scientific innovation, ecological civilization and major national development goals. The exhibition's new displays also turn to another part of the Long March story: the people who lived along the route. The objects offer a glimpse into the ties the CPC and the Red Army sought to build with local communities. Among these items are a tablecloth that Mao Zedong gave to a member of the Miao ethnic group in Guizhou, a volleyball soldiers left behind in Sichuan, and a pair of goggles presented to a guide in Yunnan. All three provinces lie in southwest China. Other artifacts include black ramie cloth and scissors given to people in Guizhou to show gratitude for their help, as well as a porcelain bowl presented to a family in Sichuan that took in a wounded soldier and cared for him as he recovered. Elsbeth van Paridon, a Dutch sinologist who joined a group retracing the Long March this past summer, said walking the route gave her a feeling similar to looking out over the beaches of Normandy and realizing what had happened there. She described the objective of the Long March as "making it all about the people." She noted that the former revolutionary sites along the route now also serve as ecological parks, becoming part of a broader tourism economy that supports local development. "That is how you see the spirit of the Long March live on," she said. The exhibition covers around 3,300 square meters and features 875 artifacts, including individual pieces and sets, along with 186 historical documents -- 1,061 items in all. It also features 357 photographs and charts and 73 artworks. Carefully designed displays recreate key episodes along the Long March, from the seizure of the Luding Bridge and the battle to break through Lazikou Pass to a meeting held in Zunyi, Guizhou, in 1935. The museum has previously staged three themed exhibitions commemorating the Long March, in 1996, 2006 and 2016. For the first time, this year's exhibition includes English-language descriptions. It will remain on display as part of the museum's permanent exhibition. ■

item.title: Extended breaks, richer experiences add momentum to China's holiday travel boom
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-03
BEIJING, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- China's National Day travel market kicked off on a strong note, as many travelers linked the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day breaks with their annual leave. This trend has led to longer trips and a surge in bookings for long-haul journeys, multi-city itineraries and experience-based travel products. LONGER BREAKS, FARTHER JOURNEYS With the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day separated by only three working days this year, some travelers used three days of leave to link the two breaks into a 13-day holiday. Trip.com Group data showed that one in every 10 travelers combined the two holidays into an extended break. Cao Shuai, CEO of Tongcheng Travel's destination business division, said strong demand for the 13-day break has lengthened the overall consumption cycle and helped release demand for long-haul and in-depth travel. Data from online travel platform Qunar showed that by Oct. 1, the first day of the National Day holiday, 20 percent of travelers had already reached the second city on their itineraries. Nearly 30 percent had booked hotels in at least two cities, while bookings involving stays in four or more cities surged 53 percent year on year. For Yuan You, who works for an internet company, the 13-day break made it possible to split one holiday into two distinct stages. She planned to first spend three days in Jiuzhaigou, a UNESCO-listed scenic area in southwest China's Sichuan Province known for its turquoise lakes and waterfalls, before continuing to Chengdu for the remainder of the break. "With such a long break, spending the whole time either resting or sightseeing can become monotonous, so I opted for a mix of both," Yuan said. In Chengdu, she chose to spend part of that extra time learning woodworking. Longer breaks are encouraging people to travel farther. Flight bookings for journeys of more than 2,000 km rose 76 percent year on year during the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day period, accounting for more than a quarter of all flight bookings, according to Meituan. Wang Peng, an associate researcher at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences, said the extended break has encouraged more people to start traveling earlier, spreading trips over a longer period rather than concentrating them within a few peak days. That, Wang said, could help sustain demand across tourism, accommodation and catering services for longer periods of time. China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway) said that China's railway network handled 25.204 million passenger trips on Oct. 1, setting a new single-day record. RICHER EXPERIENCES, MORE TO EXPLORE The surge in mobility has translated into demand for richer experiences at destinations. At the National Maritime Museum of China in north China's Tianjin Municipality, 19,000 visitors streamed through the doors on the opening day of the National Day break. Among the new draws is "Echoes of the Whale Song," the museum's first customized full-sensory virtual reality experience. Unlike conventional walk-through VR attractions, visitors remain seated as the experience unfolds around them, allowing for a more immersive encounter. Under blue lights, visitors see a giant whale entangled in discarded fishing nets and take part in a virtual rescue, learning along the way about the impact of marine debris on ocean life. Such experience-oriented products are gaining traction well beyond one museum. On Fliggy, Alibaba Group's online travel platform, domestic attraction ticket bookings on Oct. 1 rose nearly 30 percent year on year, while the number of users purchasing products for natural scenic areas and villages increased by nearly 50 percent. Searches on Qunar for "immersive performances," "fireworks shows" and "night tours" also climbed more than 50 percent year on year. The growing demand for interactive travel experiences can be seen at Changchun Zoological and Botanical Park in northeast China's Jilin Province. There, a nighttime immersive show inspired by the Chinese classic "Journey to the West" has drawn large crowds into a vibrant fantasy world, with costumed performers mingling with visitors and transforming the park into a stage after dark. Yang Han, a researcher with Qunar's big data research institute, said travelers are increasingly setting out to "enter a story" rather than simply view static scenery, with content-driven experiences gaining popularity and bringing new opportunities to less traditional tourism destinations. Bu Xiting, an associate researcher in the School of Cultural Industries Management at Communication University of China, contrasted the current trend with the previously popular "special forces-style tourism," a fast-paced form of travel in which people try to pack as many sights as possible into a short period, and city walks, which offer smaller-scale urban experiences during pockets of free time. By linking public holidays with annual leave, travelers now have more time to shape their trips around what they want to experience, Bu said. Tourism consumption, Bu noted, is shifting from a focus on "time efficiency" toward greater "experience density."■
